stimuli.text: A block of mass 3 kg on a 30° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 6 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.1. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.8 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.08\cos(2t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) and a hoop (I = MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.7 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A planet has 0.5 times Earth's mass and 0.5 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: Correct. g ∝ M/R².
g decreases with radius.
The ratio is inverted.
g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 50$$ N/m is compressed 0.15 m and launches a 0.9 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Take the square root.
The ½ appears on both sides.
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 70 kg load 18 m at constant speed in 8 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: Correct. P = mgh/t.
P = W/t.
That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 30 m is banked so that a car at 29 m/s needs no friction. What is the banking angle?

options.why: Measure the angle from the horizontal.
Correct. tan θ = v²/(rg).
Square the speed.
Use tan θ = v²/(rg), from dividing the force components.

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.2\cos(15t)$$ m. What is its maximum speed?

options.why: Correct. v_max = Aω.
That is a_max.
v_max = Aω.
Multiply by ω.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 320$$ N/m is compressed 0.19 m and launches a 0.2 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
The ½ appears on both sides.
Take the square root.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = -3t^3 - 4t^2 - 3t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 1$$ s?

options.why: Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.
Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.

questions.explanation: a(t) = -18t - 8, so at t = 1 the value is -26.

questions.stem: A 8 kg cart moving at 9 m/s collides with and sticks to a 3 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
The carts share the momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 8·9/11 = 6.55 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 88.4 J.

questions.stem: A 4 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 2t$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 3$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: The force is not constant.
Integrate the force over time.
Divide by the mass to get speed.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 9 N·s; v = J/m = 2.25 m/s.

questions.stem: A 0.7 kg ball hits a wall at 18 m/s and rebounds at 2 m/s. The contact lasts 0.1 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Include the rebound.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Divide by time.

questions.stem: A car moving at 17 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 2 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

options.why: Divide by 2a, not a.
Δx = v₀²/(2a).
That is the stopping time in seconds.
Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 40 N/m and 80 N/m are connected in series and support a 2 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Correct. k_eq = k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).
Series and parallel rules are reversed.
The force is the weight, mg.
Both springs share the load.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 5x$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 1$$ m to $$x = 2$$ m?

options.why: Correct. W = ∫F dx.
The force is not constant.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.

questions.stem: Masses of 6 kg and 3 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
Use T = m₂(g + a).
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 35° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
Friction acts up the slope.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball on a 0.5 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 4 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Include gravity.
Centripetal force uses v².
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 9 m high at 13 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Take the square root for the time.
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Fall time is √(2h/g).

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -100x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.
T = 2π/ω.
Correct. ω = √100 = 10 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.
ω is the square root of the coefficient.

questions.stem: Point masses of 2 kg and 5 kg are at the ends of a massless rod 1 m long. What is the rotational inertia about the rod's center?

options.why: Square the distance.
Measure from the center, not an end.
Each mass is L/2 from the center.
Correct. Sum of mr² with r = L/2.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 10 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 20 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Recheck the average.
The average angular speed is ω₀/2.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 2.4 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.
d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
I = mL²/3.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 5 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Friction opposes the motion.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Include friction on the table block.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 7 rad/s and amplitude 0.06 m. What is its speed when it is 0.018 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Use A² − x² under a square root.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 1x^3 - 6x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Take the square root.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 3x² − 6 = 0 gives x = 1.41 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$5 \times 10^{25}$$ kg and radius $$8 \times 10^{6}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.

questions.stem: A 14 g bullet moving at 230 m/s embeds in a 2.4 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
h = V²/(2g).

questions.explanation: V = 1.33 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.0908 m.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 4t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 4 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its velocity at $$t = 2$$ s?

options.why: That is the position.
Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.
Include the initial velocity.
Correct. Integrate a(t) and add the initial velocity.

questions.stem: A 5 kg ball moving at +9 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 6 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 6 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Only equal masses exchange velocities.
That would be a sticking collision.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
Kinetic energy is conserved too.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -0.818 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 8.18 m/s.

questions.stem: A uniform 8 m beam weighing 300 N rests on supports at both ends. A 300 N load sits 3 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
The load is not at the center.

questions.stem: A 1000 kg car heading east at 17 m/s collides with a 500 kg car heading north at 5 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Weight each velocity by its mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 0.8 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 4$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^2$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The rod is not uniform.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.9 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: The weight acts at L/2.
Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
τ = MgL/2.
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.

questions.stem: A 6 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 6 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
I/R² = M/2.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 6.53 m/s².

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 27 m/s at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its maximum height?

options.why: Only the vertical component matters.
Use the vertical component, v₀ sin θ.
Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
H = (v₀ sin θ)²/(2g).

questions.explanation: v₀x = 13.5 m/s, v₀y = 23.4 m/s. H = v₀y²/(2g) = 27.9 m.

questions.stem: An object of mass 1.6 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.01$$ kg/s. What is the time constant of its approach to terminal speed?

options.why: τ has units of seconds: m/b.
Correct. From m dv/dt = mg − bv, τ = m/b.
τ = m/b.
That is the terminal speed.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 1570 m/s and τ = m/b = 160 s.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 3 m down a 45° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.1. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Friction removes energy.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 6 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 0.7$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 4 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
W = ½Iω².
Convert revolutions to radians.
½Iω² = W; solve for ω.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 16 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).
Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).
The exponent is 3/2.
T² ∝ r³.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 6 kg and radius 0.3 m spins at 13 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1.25 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Use rotational inertias, not masses.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
The clay's inertia is mR².
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 3 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1.5 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.08 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
